solution: Every element of \(A\) is joined to exactly one element of \(B\): \(2 \to -3\), \(1 \to 1\), \(0 \to 2\), \(-1 \to 1\), \(-2 \to 5\). No element of \(A\) is left out and none has two images. (Two different elements \(1\) and \(-1\) having the same image \(1\) is permitted.) Hence the relation is a function.

The element \(r\) of \(A\) is joined to two elements of \(B\), namely \(b\) and \(d\), so \(r\) has two images. A function must assign exactly one image to each element of the domain. Hence the relation is not a function.
The element \(-2\) of \(A\) is not joined to any element of \(B\), so it has no image. A function must assign an image to every element of its domain. Hence the relation is not a function.

The element \(2\) occurs as the first component of two ordered pairs, \((2, -1)\) and \((2, 2)\), so \(2\) would have two images \(-1\) and \(2\). A function cannot assign two images to one element. Hence this set does not represent a function.

The first components are \(1, 2, 3, 4\), so every element of \(A\) occurs exactly once, and the images \(2, -1, 1, 3\) all belong to \(B\). Each element of \(A\) therefore has exactly one image in \(B\). Hence this set represents a function from \(A\) to \(B\).

The first components are only \(1, 4, 2\); the element \(3 \in A\) does not appear, so \(3\) has no image. A function must be defined at every element of its domain. Hence this set does not represent a function.

Each of \(1, 2, 3, 4\) occurs exactly once as a first component, and the image \(1\) belongs to \(B\). Different elements of the domain are allowed to have the same image, so nothing is violated. Hence this set represents a function from \(A\) to \(B\), namely the constant function \(f(x) = 1\).

\(2x + 3y = 12 \Rightarrow 3y = 12 - 2x \Rightarrow y = \frac{12 - 2x}{3}\). For each real value of \(x\) this expression gives exactly one value of \(y\). Hence the equation represents \(y\) as a function of \(x\).

\(x + y^2 = 9 \Rightarrow y^2 = 9 - x \Rightarrow y = \pm\sqrt{9 - x}\). For example \(x = 0\) gives both \(y = 3\) and \(y = -3\), so one value of \(x\) has two values of \(y\). Hence the equation does not represent \(y\) as a function of \(x\).
\(x^2 - y = 25 \Rightarrow y = x^2 - 25\). For each real value of \(x\) this gives exactly one value of \(y\). Hence the equation represents \(y\) as a function of \(x\).

\(2y + 10 = 0 \Rightarrow y = -5\). Whatever value \(x\) takes, \(y\) has the single value \(-5\); this is the constant function \(y = -5\). Hence the equation represents \(y\) as a function of \(x\).

\(3x - 6 = 21 \Rightarrow 3x = 27 \Rightarrow x = 9\). The equation places no condition on \(y\) at all: for \(x = 9\) every real \(y\) satisfies it (infinitely many images), and for \(x \ne 9\) no value of \(y\) satisfies it. Hence the equation does not represent \(y\) as a function of \(x\).
Put \(m = \frac{1}{2}\) in \(f(m) = m^2 - 3m + 1\): \(f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{4} - \frac{3}{2} + 1 = \frac{1 - 6 + 4}{4}\). Therefore \(f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = -\frac{1}{4}\).
\(g(x) = 0 \Rightarrow \frac{5x - 6}{7} = 0 \Rightarrow 5x - 6 = 0 \Rightarrow 5x = 6\). Therefore \(x = \frac{6}{5}\).
\(g(x) = 0 \Rightarrow \frac{18 - 2x^2}{7} = 0 \Rightarrow 18 - 2x^2 = 0 \Rightarrow x^2 = 9\). Therefore \(x = \pm 3\).

\(6x^2 + x - 2 = 0\). Splitting the middle term, \(6x^2 + 4x - 3x - 2 = 0 \Rightarrow 2x(3x + 2) - (3x + 2) = 0 \Rightarrow (3x + 2)(2x - 1) = 0\). Therefore \(x = \frac{1}{2}\) or \(x = -\frac{2}{3}\).
\(f(x) = g(x) \Rightarrow x^4 + 2x^2 = 11x^2 \Rightarrow x^4 - 9x^2 = 0 \Rightarrow x^2(x^2 - 9) = 0\). So \(x^2 = 0\) or \(x^2 = 9\). Therefore \(x = 0\) or \(x = \pm 3\).

\(f(x) = g(x) \Rightarrow \sqrt{x} - 3 = 5 - x \Rightarrow \sqrt{x} = 8 - x\). This needs \(x \ge 0\) and \(8 - x \ge 0\), i.e. \(0 \le x \le 8\). Squaring, \(x = 64 - 16x + x^2 \Rightarrow x^2 - 17x + 64 = 0\), so \(x = \frac{17 \pm \sqrt{289 - 256}}{2} = \frac{17 \pm \sqrt{33}}{2}\). Now \(\frac{17 + \sqrt{33}}{2} \approx 11.37 > 8\), which violates \(\sqrt{x} = 8 - x \ge 0\), so it is an extraneous root introduced by squaring. Checking \(\frac{17 - \sqrt{33}}{2} \approx 5.63\): \(\sqrt{5.63} - 3 \approx -0.63\) and \(5 - 5.63 \approx -0.63\), which agree. Therefore \(x = \frac{17 - \sqrt{33}}{2}\).
_note: The book's key gives both roots \(\frac{17 \pm \sqrt{33}}{2}\). Only \(\frac{17 - \sqrt{33}}{2}\) satisfies the original equation; \(\frac{17 + \sqrt{33}}{2} \approx 11.37\) makes the right side \(5 - x \approx -6.37\) while the left side \(\sqrt{x} - 3 \approx 0.37\), so it is extraneous (introduced by squaring). Book answer-key error.

solution: \(f(x) = \frac{a - x}{b - x}\) is undefined exactly where the denominator vanishes. Since \(f(2)\) is undefined, \(b - 2 = 0\), so \(b = 2\). Then \(f(3) = \frac{a - 3}{2 - 3} = \frac{a - 3}{-1} = 3 - a\). Given \(f(3) = 5\), \(3 - a = 5 \Rightarrow a = -2\). Therefore \(a = -2\) and \(b = 2\).

\(f(x) = 7x^2 + 4x - 1\) is a polynomial, so it is defined for every real \(x\): domain \(= \mathbb{R}\). Completing the square, \(f(x) = 7\left(x + \frac{2}{7}\right)^2 - \frac{11}{7}\), whose least value is \(-\frac{11}{7}\) at \(x = -\frac{2}{7}\), and which increases without bound. Therefore domain \(= \mathbb{R}\), range \(= \left[-\frac{11}{7}, \infty\right)\).

\(g(x) = \frac{x + 4}{x - 2}\) is defined for all \(x\) except \(x = 2\), so domain \(= \mathbb{R} - \{2\}\). For the range put \(y = \frac{x + 4}{x - 2}\): \(y(x - 2) = x + 4 \Rightarrow x(y - 1) = 2y + 4 \Rightarrow x = \frac{2y + 4}{y - 1}\), which gives a real \(x\) for every \(y\) except \(y = 1\). Therefore domain \(= \mathbb{R} - \{2\}\), range \(= \mathbb{R} - \{1\}\).

\(h(x) = \frac{\sqrt{x + 5}}{5 + x} = \frac{\sqrt{x + 5}}{(\sqrt{x + 5})^2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x + 5}}\). This needs \(x + 5 > 0\) (it must be non-negative for the radical and non-zero for the denominator), i.e. \(x > -5\). As \(x\) runs over \((-5, \infty)\), \(\sqrt{x + 5}\) takes every positive value, so \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x + 5}}\) also takes every positive value. Therefore domain \(= (-5, \infty)\), range \(= (0, \infty) = \mathbb{R}^{+}\).

\(f(x) = \sqrt[3]{x + 1} = (x + 1)^{1/3}\). A cube root is defined for every real number, so domain \(= \mathbb{R}\). Given any real \(y\), \(x = y^3 - 1\) gives \(f(x) = y\), so every real value is attained. Therefore domain \(= \mathbb{R}\), range \(= \mathbb{R}\).

\(f(x) = \sqrt{(x - 2)(5 - x)}\) needs \((x - 2)(5 - x) \ge 0\), which holds for \(2 \le x \le 5\): domain \(= [2, 5]\). Writing \((x - 2)(5 - x) = -\left(x - \frac{7}{2}\right)^2 + \frac{9}{4}\), the expression runs from \(0\) (at \(x = 2, 5\)) up to \(\frac{9}{4}\) (at \(x = \frac{7}{2}\)). Taking square roots, \(f(x)\) runs from \(0\) to \(\frac{3}{2}\). Therefore domain \(= [2, 5]\), range \(= \left[0, \frac{3}{2}\right]\).

\(f(x) = \sqrt{\frac{x - 3}{7 - x}}\) needs \(\frac{x - 3}{7 - x} \ge 0\) with \(7 - x \ne 0\), which holds for \(3 \le x < 7\): domain \(= [3, 7)\). On this interval \(\frac{x - 3}{7 - x}\) equals \(0\) at \(x = 3\) and increases without bound as \(x \to 7^{-}\), so it takes every value in \([0, \infty)\), and so does its square root. Therefore domain \(= [3, 7)\), range \(= [0, \infty)\).
_note: The book's key prints the range as \([0, \infty]\) with a closed bracket at infinity; \(\infty\) is not a value the function attains, so the correct notation is \([0, \infty)\). Typesetting slip in the key, not a mathematical disagreement.

solution: \(f(x) = \sqrt{16 - x^2}\) needs \(16 - x^2 \ge 0\), i.e. \(x^2 \le 16\), i.e. \(-4 \le x \le 4\): domain \(= [-4, 4]\). On this interval \(16 - x^2\) runs from \(0\) (at \(x = \pm 4\)) to \(16\) (at \(x = 0\)), so \(f(x)\) runs from \(0\) to \(4\). Therefore domain \(= [-4, 4]\), range \(= [0, 4]\).
A square of side \(s\) has area equal to the product of its two equal sides. Therefore \(A = s^2\).
If the perimeter is \(P\) then \(P = 4s\), so \(s = \frac{P}{4}\). Substituting in \(A = s^2\), \(A = \left(\frac{P}{4}\right)^2\). Therefore \(A = \frac{P^2}{16}\).
The area of a circle of radius \(r\) is \(\pi\) times the square of the radius. Therefore \(A = \pi r^2\).
If the diameter is \(d\) then \(r = \frac{d}{2}\). Substituting in \(A = \pi r^2\), \(A = \pi \left(\frac{d}{2}\right)^2\). Therefore \(A = \frac{\pi d^2}{4}\).
If the circumference is \(C\) then \(C = 2\pi r\), so \(r = \frac{C}{2\pi}\). Substituting in \(A = \pi r^2\), \(A = \pi \cdot \frac{C^2}{4\pi^2}\). Therefore \(A = \frac{C^2}{4\pi}\).

Squares of side \(x\) are cut from each corner of a square sheet of side \(30\) cm, so each side of the sheet loses \(x\) at both ends. The base of the open box is a square of side \(30 - 2x\) and the height of the box is \(x\). So the volume is \(V(x) = x(30 - 2x)^2\). For an actual box we need \(x > 0\) and \(30 - 2x > 0\), i.e. \(x < 15\). Therefore \(V(x) = x(30 - 2x)^2\) cubic cm, with domain \((0, 15)\).

For \(f\) to be a function from \(Z\) to \(Z\), each first component must have exactly one image. Take \(a = 0, b = 1\): this gives the pair \((0 \cdot 1,\; 0 + 1) = (0, 1)\). Take \(a = 0, b = 2\): this gives \((0 \cdot 2,\; 0 + 2) = (0, 2)\). So the element \(0\) is paired with both \(1\) and \(2\), i.e. \(f(0)\) has more than one value. Therefore \(f\) is not a function from \(Z\) to \(Z\).

Let \(x_1, x_2 \in N\) with \(f(x_1) = f(x_2)\), i.e. \(x_1^2 = x_2^2\). Since \(x_1, x_2\) are positive, this gives \(x_1 = x_2\), so \(f\) is injective. For surjectivity, \(2 \in N\) (codomain) but there is no \(x \in N\) with \(x^2 = 2\), since \(2\) is not a perfect square. Therefore \(f\) is injective but not surjective.

Here \(f(1) = 1 = f(-1)\) with \(1 \ne -1\), so \(f\) is not injective. Also \(-1 \in Z\) (codomain) has no preimage, since \(x^2 \ge 0\) for every \(x \in Z\), so \(f\) is not surjective. Therefore \(f\) is neither injective nor surjective.

Here \(f(2) = 4 = f(-2)\) with \(2 \ne -2\), so \(f\) is not injective. Also \(-4 \in \mathbb{R}\) (codomain) has no preimage, since \(x^2 \ge 0\) for every real \(x\), so \(f\) is not surjective. Therefore \(f\) is neither injective nor surjective.

Let \(x_1, x_2 \in N\) with \(x_1^3 = x_2^3\); taking cube roots gives \(x_1 = x_2\), so \(f\) is injective. For surjectivity, \(2 \in N\) (codomain) has no preimage in \(N\), since \(2\) is not a perfect cube. Therefore \(f\) is injective but not surjective.

If \(x_1^3 = x_2^3\) then taking real cube roots gives \(x_1 = x_2\), so \(f\) is injective. Given any \(y \in \mathbb{R}\), the number \(x = \sqrt[3]{y}\) is real and satisfies \(f(x) = y\), so every element of the codomain has a preimage and \(f\) is surjective. Therefore \(f\) is both injective and surjective (i.e. bijective).

Let \(x_1, x_2 \in A\) with \((g \circ f)(x_1) = (g \circ f)(x_2)\), that is \(g\big(f(x_1)\big) = g\big(f(x_2)\big)\). Since \(g\) is one-one and \(f(x_1), f(x_2) \in B\), this gives \(f(x_1) = f(x_2)\). Since \(f\) is one-one, this gives \(x_1 = x_2\). Thus \((g \circ f)(x_1) = (g \circ f)(x_2)\) forces \(x_1 = x_2\). Hence \(g \circ f : A \to C\) is one-one.

Let \(z \in C\) be arbitrary. Since \(g : B \to C\) is onto, there exists \(y \in B\) with \(g(y) = z\). Since \(f : A \to B\) is onto, there exists \(x \in A\) with \(f(x) = y\). Then \((g \circ f)(x) = g\big(f(x)\big) = g(y) = z\). So every element of \(C\) has a preimage in \(A\) under \(g \circ f\). Hence \(g \circ f : A \to C\) is onto.
By the definition of a logarithm, \(a^b = c\) is equivalent to \(\log_a c = b\). Here \(2^5 = 32\). Therefore \(\log_2 32 = 5\).
Using \(a^b = c \Leftrightarrow \log_a c = b\) with \(54^0 = 1\). Therefore \(\log_{54} 1 = 0\).
Using \(a^b = c \Leftrightarrow \log_a c = b\) with \(23^1 = 23\). Therefore \(\log_{23} 23 = 1\).
Using \(a^b = c \Leftrightarrow \log_a c = b\) with \(9^{3/2} = 27\). Therefore \(\log_9 27 = \frac{3}{2}\).
Using \(a^b = c \Leftrightarrow \log_a c = b\) with \(3^{-4} = \frac{1}{81}\). Therefore \(\log_3\left(\frac{1}{81}\right) = -4\).
Using \(a^b = c \Leftrightarrow \log_a c = b\) with \(10^{-2} = 0.01\). Therefore \(\log_{10} 0.01 = -2\).
A logarithm to the base \(e\) is written \(\ln\), so \(e^b = c \Leftrightarrow \ln c = b\). Here \(e^2 = 7.3890\). Therefore \(\ln 7.3890 = 2\).
Using \(e^b = c \Leftrightarrow \ln c = b\) with \(e^{1/2} = 1.6487\). Therefore \(\ln 1.6487 = \frac{1}{2}\).
Using \(e^b = c \Leftrightarrow \ln c = b\) with \(e^{-x} = 6\). Therefore \(\ln 6 = -x\).
By the definition of a logarithm, \(\log_a c = b\) is equivalent to \(a^b = c\). Here \(\log_2 64 = 6\). Therefore \(2^6 = 64\).
Using \(\log_a c = b \Leftrightarrow a^b = c\) with \(\log_5 \frac{1}{25} = -2\). Therefore \(5^{-2} = \frac{1}{25}\).
Using \(\log_a c = b \Leftrightarrow a^b = c\) with \(\log_{10} 0.001 = -3\). Therefore \(10^{-3} = 0.001\).

As printed the statement is \(\log_{1/2}(-8) = 3\), which cannot be right: a logarithm is not defined for a negative number, and \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \frac{1}{8}\), not \(8\). The minus sign has been typeset on the \(8\) instead of on the \(3\); the intended statement is \(\log_{1/2} 8 = -3\). Using \(\log_a c = b \Leftrightarrow a^b = c\) on that, \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-3} = 2^3 = 8\). Therefore \(8 = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-3}\).
_note: Known book misprint (already adjudicated): the stem prints \(\log_{1/2}(-8) = 3\), false twice over (negative argument, and \((1/2)^3 = 1/8\)). The book's own key answers \(8 = (1/2)^{-3}\), i.e. it reads the question as \(\log_{1/2} 8 = -3\) — the minus was typeset onto the \(8\) instead of the \(3\). Solved in the intended form and the defect is stated in the solution.

solution: Using \(\ln c = b \Leftrightarrow e^b = c\) with \(\ln 1 = 0\). Therefore \(e^0 = 1\).
Using \(\ln c = b \Leftrightarrow e^b = c\) with \(\ln e = 1\). Therefore \(e^1 = e\).
Using \(\ln c = b \Leftrightarrow e^b = c\) with \(\ln \frac{1}{2} = -0.693\). Therefore \(e^{-0.693} = \frac{1}{2}\).
\(\ln(x - 5)\) is defined only when its argument is positive, so \(x - 5 > 0\), i.e. \(x > 5\). Therefore the domain is \((5, \infty)\).

We need \(x^2 - 5x + 6 > 0\), i.e. \((x - 2)(x - 3) > 0\). The product of the two factors is positive when both are negative (\(x < 2\)) or both are positive (\(x > 3\)). Therefore the domain is \((-\infty, 2) \cup (3, \infty)\).

Using \(\log(mn) = \log m + \log n\) and \(\log\left(\frac{m}{n}\right) = \log m - \log n\): \(\log\left(\frac{pq}{rs}\right) = \log(pq) - \log(rs)\). Therefore \(\log\left(\frac{pq}{rs}\right) = \log p + \log q - \log r - \log s\).

Write the radicals as powers: \(\sqrt{x}\,\sqrt[3]{y} = x^{1/2} y^{1/3}\). Using \(\log(mn) = \log m + \log n\) and \(\log m^k = k \log m\), \(\log\left(x^{1/2} y^{1/3}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\log x + \frac{1}{3}\log y\). Therefore \(\log\left(\sqrt{x}\,\sqrt[3]{y}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\log x + \frac{1}{3}\log y\).

\(\ln\left(\frac{a^3 (a-2)^2}{\sqrt{b^2+5}}\right) = \ln a^3 + \ln (a-2)^2 - \ln (b^2+5)^{1/2}\), using \(\ln(mn) = \ln m + \ln n\) and \(\ln\left(\frac{m}{n}\right) = \ln m - \ln n\). Now applying \(\ln m^k = k \ln m\) to each term, this equals \(3\ln a + 2\ln(a-2) - \frac{1}{2}\ln(b^2+5)\).

First bring the outer index down: \(\ln\left[\frac{\sqrt[3]{x-2}\,(2x+1)^4}{(x+4)\sqrt{2x+4}}\right]^2 = 2\ln\left[\frac{(x-2)^{1/3}(2x+1)^4}{(x+4)(2x+4)^{1/2}}\right]\). Splitting the numerator and denominator by \(\ln(mn) = \ln m + \ln n\) and \(\ln\frac{m}{n} = \ln m - \ln n\), and then using \(\ln m^k = k\ln m\), this equals \(2\left[\frac{1}{3}\ln(x-2) + 4\ln(2x+1) - \ln(x+4) - \frac{1}{2}\ln(2x+4)\right]\).

Using \(k\log m = \log m^k\), \(5\log x + 7\log y - \log z = \log x^5 + \log y^7 - \log z\). Then combining by \(\log m + \log n = \log(mn)\) and \(\log m - \log n = \log\frac{m}{n}\), this equals \(\log\left(\frac{x^5 y^7}{z}\right)\).

Using \(k\log m = \log m^k\), \(\frac{1}{3}\log(x-1) + \frac{1}{2}\log x = \log (x-1)^{1/3} + \log x^{1/2}\). Adding by \(\log m + \log n = \log(mn)\), this equals \(\log\left(\sqrt[3]{x-1}\,\sqrt{x}\right)\).

\(\ln(x+2) + \ln(x-2) - 3\ln(x+5) = \ln\big[(x+2)(x-2)\big] - \ln (x+5)^3\), using \(\ln m + \ln n = \ln(mn)\) and \(k\ln m = \ln m^k\). Since \((x+2)(x-2) = x^2 - 4\), and using \(\ln m - \ln n = \ln\frac{m}{n}\), this equals \(\ln\left[\frac{x^2 - 4}{(x+5)^3}\right]\).

\(\log \sqrt{96} = \log 96^{1/2} = \frac{1}{2}\log 96\). Now \(96 = 32 \times 3 = 2^5 \times 3\), so \(\log 96 = \log 2^5 + \log 3 = 5\log 2 + \log 3 = 5a + b\). Therefore \(\log \sqrt{96} = \frac{5a + b}{2}\).
Let \(\log_b a = t\). By the definition of a logarithm this means \(b^t = a\). Substituting \(t\) back into the left side, \(b^{\log_b a} = b^t = a\). Hence \(b^{\log_b a} = a\).

Let \(\log_{b^m} a = t\). By the definition of a logarithm, \((b^m)^t = a\), i.e. \(b^{mt} = a\). Converting this back to logarithmic form to the base \(b\) gives \(mt = \log_b a\), so \(t = \frac{1}{m}\log_b a\). Hence \(\log_{b^m} a = \frac{1}{m}\log_b a\).

Take \(\log_c\) of the left side: \(\log_c\left(a^{\log_c b}\right) = (\log_c b)(\log_c a)\), using \(\log_c m^k = k\log_c m\). Take \(\log_c\) of the right side: \(\log_c\left(b^{\log_c a}\right) = (\log_c a)(\log_c b)\). The two results are the same product, so the two logarithms are equal. Since the logarithm function is one-one, the numbers themselves are equal. Hence \(a^{\log_c b} = b^{\log_c a}\).

\(\log 2 + \log(x+3) - \log(3x-5) = \log 3 \Rightarrow \log\left[\frac{2(x+3)}{3x-5}\right] = \log 3\). Since \(\log\) is one-one, \(\frac{2(x+3)}{3x-5} = 3 \Rightarrow 2x + 6 = 9x - 15 \Rightarrow 7x = 21\). So \(x = 3\), and this is admissible since \(x + 3 = 6 > 0\) and \(3x - 5 = 4 > 0\). Therefore \(x = 3\).

\(2\log_{10} x = 1 + \log_{10}\left(x + \frac{11}{10}\right) \Rightarrow \log_{10} x^2 = \log_{10} 10 + \log_{10}\left(x + \frac{11}{10}\right) = \log_{10}\left[10\left(x + \frac{11}{10}\right)\right] = \log_{10}(10x + 11)\). Since \(\log\) is one-one, \(x^2 = 10x + 11 \Rightarrow x^2 - 10x - 11 = 0 \Rightarrow (x - 11)(x + 1) = 0\), so \(x = 11\) or \(x = -1\). But \(\log_{10} x\) requires \(x > 0\), so \(x = -1\) is rejected. Therefore \(x = 11\).

Using \(\log_{b^m} a = \frac{1}{m}\log_b a\): \(\log_4 x = \log_{2^2} x = \frac{1}{2}\log_2 x\) and \(\log_{16} x = \log_{2^4} x = \frac{1}{4}\log_2 x\). Put \(t = \log_2 x\); the equation becomes \(t + \frac{t}{2} + \frac{t}{4} = \frac{21}{4}\), i.e. \(\frac{7t}{4} = \frac{21}{4}\), so \(t = 3\). Then \(\log_2 x = 3 \Rightarrow x = 2^3\). Therefore \(x = 8\).

Rearranging, \(x - x\log_{10} 5 = \log_{10} 6 - \log_{10}(1 + 2^x)\), i.e. \(x\left(1 - \log_{10} 5\right) = \log_{10}\left(\frac{6}{1 + 2^x}\right)\). Now \(1 - \log_{10} 5 = \log_{10} 10 - \log_{10} 5 = \log_{10} 2\), so the left side is \(x\log_{10} 2 = \log_{10} 2^x\). Hence \(\log_{10} 2^x = \log_{10}\left(\frac{6}{1 + 2^x}\right) \Rightarrow 2^x\left(1 + 2^x\right) = 6\). Putting \(u = 2^x\), \(u^2 + u - 6 = 0 \Rightarrow (u + 3)(u - 2) = 0\), and \(u = 2^x > 0\) forces \(u = 2\). So \(2^x = 2\). Therefore \(x = 1\).

\(\frac{1}{2}\log x + \frac{1}{2}\log y = \frac{1}{2}\log(xy) = \log \sqrt{xy}\), so the given equation is \(\log\left(\frac{x+y}{3}\right) = \log \sqrt{xy}\). Since \(\log\) is one-one, \(\frac{x+y}{3} = \sqrt{xy}\), i.e. \(x + y = 3\sqrt{xy}\). Squaring both sides, \(x^2 + 2xy + y^2 = 9xy\), so \(x^2 + y^2 = 7xy\). Dividing throughout by \(xy\) (which is positive, since \(\log x\) and \(\log y\) require \(x, y > 0\)), \(\frac{x}{y} + \frac{y}{x} = 7\). Hence \(\frac{x}{y} + \frac{y}{x} = 7\).

\(\log \sqrt{x} + \log \sqrt{y} = \log\left(\sqrt{x}\sqrt{y}\right) = \log \sqrt{xy}\), so the given equation is \(\log\left(\frac{x-y}{4}\right) = \log \sqrt{xy}\). Since \(\log\) is one-one, \(\frac{x-y}{4} = \sqrt{xy}\), i.e. \(x - y = 4\sqrt{xy}\). Squaring, \(x^2 - 2xy + y^2 = 16xy\), so \(x^2 + y^2 = 18xy\). Then \((x+y)^2 = x^2 + 2xy + y^2 = 18xy + 2xy = 20xy\). Hence \((x+y)^2 = 20xy\).

\(1 + x = \log_a a + \log_a bc = \log_a(abc)\), so \(\frac{1}{1+x} = \frac{1}{\log_a(abc)} = \log_{abc} a\), using \(\frac{1}{\log_p q} = \log_q p\). Similarly \(1 + y = \log_b b + \log_b ca = \log_b(abc)\), giving \(\frac{1}{1+y} = \log_{abc} b\), and \(1 + z = \log_c c + \log_c ab = \log_c(abc)\), giving \(\frac{1}{1+z} = \log_{abc} c\). Adding, \(\frac{1}{1+x} + \frac{1}{1+y} + \frac{1}{1+z} = \log_{abc} a + \log_{abc} b + \log_{abc} c = \log_{abc}(abc) = 1\). Hence the required sum is \(1\).
